prompt: On a fresh Ubuntu container, `apt-get install -y curl` fails with "Unable to locate package curl" until you first run `apt-get update`. What does that update step actually do?
choices: It downloads and applies security patches to the OS automatically
It refreshes apt's local index of available packages and versions from the configured repositories, which a fresh system doesn't have yet
It upgrades every already-installed package to its newest version
It accepts the package manager's license agreement for this session

prompt: Why do unattended provisioning scripts for Ubuntu set `export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive` before calling `apt-get install`?
choices: It makes package downloads transfer faster
It suppresses interactive configuration prompts that would otherwise hang the script forever waiting for input no one is there to give
It disables GPG signature verification for downloaded packages
It allows apt to install packages without specifying their names

prompt: You're writing a Dockerfile that starts `FROM alpine:3.19` and need to install curl. Which command is correct for that base image?
choices: apt-get install -y curl
brew install curl
apk add --no-cache curl
winget install curl

prompt: Which statement correctly describes Homebrew and winget in an ops/provisioning context?
choices: Both are the standard tools for provisioning production Linux servers
Homebrew is the default package manager on Amazon Linux and RHEL
They are primarily personal-workstation tools (macOS and Windows client, respectively); a fresh Linux server or container typically uses apt, dnf/yum, or apk instead
Installing winget on a Linux server replaces apt entirely

prompt: A teammate runs your setup script on a brand-new VM and it fails with "python3.11: command not found," even though the exact same script works on your laptop. What's the most likely root cause?
choices: The VM's filesystem is corrupted
The script quietly depended on something already present on your machine (a repo, package, or PATH entry you set up manually at some point) that was never captured in the script itself
VMs are generally unable to run Python
The teammate's VM needs more CPU cores to run apt

prompt: What's the most reliable way to verify a provisioning script is genuinely reproducible, not just "works on my machine"?
choices: Read through the script carefully one more time
Ask a senior engineer whether it looks correct
Run it a second time on your own machine
Run it from scratch inside a fresh, disposable environment (a new container or VM) that shares none of your machine's prior state

prompt: Why pin exact package versions (e.g., `curl=7.81.0-1ubuntu1.15`) in a provisioning script instead of just naming the package?
choices: Pinned versions always download faster
Without pinning, "latest" drifts over time, so the identical script can produce a different, potentially broken environment weeks or months later
Package managers require a version number to run at all
Pinning only matters for Python packages installed with pip, not for apt packages
